analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run Medicare drug plan that negotiates drug prices directly with manufacturers.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote; it died in subcommittee when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let Medicare itself offer a nationwide prescription drug plan alongside the private plans in Medicare Part D. Medicare would negotiate drug prices directly with pharmaceutical companies and use VA-style purchasing strategies, and the savings would fill the coverage gap known as the donut hole. Seniors could enroll at any time with a single national premium and no late-enrollment penalty.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, especially those who fall into the Part D coverage gap and pay full price for drugs there. A government-run plan negotiating directly with manufacturers would offer lower prices, a uniform national premium, and enrollment at any time.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries paying high drug prices

how_it_helps.text: Medicare would offer its own nationwide drug plan whose prices are negotiated directly with pharmaceutical manufacturers, rather than relying only on private plans and pharmacy benefit intermediaries.

The plan would use cost-saving strategies similar to those of the Department of Veterans Affairs and other federal purchasers, and encourage cheaper therapeutic equivalents where medically appropriate.
Savings from negotiation would be used to extend coverage to people who have hit the initial coverage limit but not yet reached the out-of-pocket threshold, softening the donut hole.
Enrollees would pay a nationally uniform premium and could enroll at any time without a late-enrollment penalty, unlike standard Part D rules.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers would face a purchaser with negotiating leverage for the first time in Medicare Part D, and private Part D insurance companies would face a government-run competitor for enrollment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug makers and private Part D insurers

drawbacks.text: Direct government negotiation and a public plan competitor would reduce pharmaceutical revenue, which the industry argues funds research and development of new drugs; the bill text explicitly overrides the Part D 'non-interference' provision that bars Medicare from negotiating prices.

A Medicare-operated plan competing with private Part D plans could draw enrollment away from private insurers and reshape the Part D market, raising concerns about private plans' ability to compete and about government advantages in bidding.
Drug savings depend on manufacturers actually agreeing to lower prices in negotiation; the bill gives Medicare leverage but does not guarantee the magnitude of savings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For seniors in the donut hole and taxpayers concerned about drug prices, the potential gains were substantial: lower negotiated prices and savings redirected to fill the coverage gap. The main costs fall on drug manufacturers and private Part D insurers, whose business models would face a new government competitor. The design is voluntary and preserves private plans, so the tradeoff is mostly a contest over who controls drug purchasing leverage — the government on behalf of beneficiaries, or manufacturers and private intermediaries.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to a Health subcommittee, and neither committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Christopher Murphy of Connecticut introduced the bill on June 12, 2009, joined by Rep. Joe Courtney as its sole cosponsor.
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced.
Three days later it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, where its action history ends.
No markup, committee vote, floor vote, or further action of any kind is recorded before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and private Part D insurers are better off, because Medicare never gained the authority to negotiate drug prices or compete with them directly, and the Part D market they operate remained unchanged. Medicare beneficiaries gained nothing from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and private drug plans

for.name: Rep. Christopher Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a Medicare-operated drug plan with negotiated prices.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee of primary referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or acted on the bill after its referral to the Health subcommittee.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee of secondary referral
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after receiving the referral.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: Opposed letting the government negotiate Medicare drug prices; during the 2009 health care debate the industry campaigned to keep government price negotiation out of the health overhaul.

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats are on the record — one sponsor and one cosponsor among the 253 House Democrats — and no vote was ever recorded, so the partisan shape of the bill's death cannot be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill would have repealed Part D's 'non-interference' clause for the public plan and required Medicare to negotiate purchase prices directly, the leverage drug makers have successfully resisted since Part D was created. Lower negotiated prices would come directly out of manufacturer revenue.

A Medicare-operated plan available nationwide with a uniform premium and open enrollment would compete directly for Part D enrollment against private plans, which currently are the only option and collectively serve every Part D beneficiary. Insurers would lose market share or be forced to match the public plan's prices.
